title: Judicial Renaissance -- Ch. 12: An Ethical Compass for the Legal Profession
keywords: Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr.
primary_topics: Chapter 12 of 'Judicial Renaissance' -- the address CJP delivered at the induction of the IBP-Pampanga Chapter officers, sounding a call to ethics for the legal profession amid what he called the country's crisis of confidence and credibility.

The three ethical virtues he anatomizes -- fairness (refusing to take undue advantage of the other side), candor (straightforwardness in admitting weakness or error), and integrity (acting on what is true and honest regardless of personal consequences) -- as values enshrined in the Code of Professional Responsibility.

The Supreme Court's increasing strictness in disciplining lawyers under Chief Justice Davide: 463 lawyers sanctioned from 1999 to 2004, illustrated by three recent disciplinary cases ending in disbarment or rebuke.

The hierarchy of a lawyer's loyalties -- fidelity to the courts before self-interest, to truth before the client's cause -- and the mariner's-compass image of an ethical bearing that always points to the same north.
sub_topics: CJP thanks Judge Irin Zenaida S. Buan for introducing him by analyzing his legal philosophy from his decisions rather than reciting the usual biographical milestones.
He praises the new breed of young, competent and honest magistrates in Pampanga and notes that Pampango judges always shine when the justices discuss rising stars.

He recalls that Kapampangans have distinguished themselves in a century of Philippine judicial history, above all Chief Justice Jose Abad Santos, who chose martyrdom over collaboration, and Chief Justice Cayetano Arellano -- the two honored with statues at the Court's gate.

He recounts that when he joined the Supreme Court in 1995 seven of fifteen members were Pampangeños and all five members of his Third Division were cabalens -- the 'Lahar Division' -- of which he is now the only survivor.

He thanks Atty. Josep Jepri M. Miranda and Atty. Jose Songco, and gives his reasons for accepting: the chance to speak the dialect, the Kapampangan delicacies, and above all his geographic and professional kinship with the audience.
Fairness is defined as more than even-handed treatment: it is refusing undue advantage, being honorable in battle and scrupulous in the choice of legal weapons.
He illustrates fairness with the 1960 trial in which Atty. Jose W. Diokno moved to postpone the hearing rather than cross-examine an unprepared young substitute counsel.
Candor is defined as forthrightness in admitting weakness or error, including the honesty to concede that a passage is a mere obiter rather than ratio decidendi.
He warns that nothing erodes credibility more than misquoting a decision or omitting qualifying words, since eagle-eyed magistrates detect misquotations and misleading arguments.
Integrity is honesty and truthfulness acted upon regardless of personal consequences -- moral courage that presupposes purity of spirit and clarity of conscience.
He asks the bar's help in eradicating corruption and incompetence on the bench, since lawyers know which judges do not deserve their robes, and insists lawyers of integrity never bribe a judge.

He condemns lawyers who collect money from clients ostensibly to pay off magistrates, and those who harass decent judges with baseless administrative complaints that stall promotions before the Judicial and Bar Council.
He reports Office of the Bar Confidant figures for 1999-2004: 463 lawyers disciplined -- 23 disbarred, 138 suspended, 155 fined, 57 reprimanded, 50 admonished, and 14 notarial commissions suspended.

He summarizes three recent disciplinary cases: a lawyer disbarred for abetting perjury and forgery in his parents-in-law's estate; a former judge disbarred for obstinate immorality; and a counsel rebuked for deceiving a trial court about a missing signature on a Compromise Agreement.
He quotes Justice J. B. L. Reyes on keeping one's soul attuned to morality and honor, and develops the mariner's compass as the figure for constant ethical bearing.
He warns against lawyers who have become mere legal technicians and have jumbled the hierarchy of responsibilities, putting their own interests first and justice a far third.

He notes that the Court tracks lawyers' conduct: counsels' names appear on the Court's agenda, their arguments are discussed among the justices, and he footnotes the names of opposing counsel in his own ponencias.
He closes by promising to remember the names of IBP-Pampanga members and to speak well of them, urging cabalen attorneys to keep no compass but ethics.

stances.claim: Fairness requires more than fighting for even-handed treatment; it means refusing to take undue advantage of the other side, being honorable in battle and scrupulous in the choice of legal weapons.
stances.rhetorical_move: definition followed by a first-hand exemplar -- Diokno's voluntary motion to postpone rather than cross-examine an unprepared young lawyer

stances.claim: Corruption in the judiciary will take place only if it is abetted or tolerated by the bar, so lawyers of integrity must both denounce the corrupt and defend the decent from scurrilous attacks.
stances.rhetorical_move: shifting responsibility onto the audience and pairing the duty to denounce with a symmetrical duty to defend

stances.claim: A lawyer's fidelity runs to the courts before self-interest and to truth before the client's cause; those who invert this hierarchy are more to be feared than the criminals they defend.
stances.rhetorical_move: explicit ranking of values, sharpened by the paradox that legal knowledge without morality is more dangerous than criminality

stances.claim: The Supreme Court under Chief Justice Davide has become uncompromising in disciplining lawyers, and the resulting numbers reflect badly on the moral fiber of present-day lawyers.
stances.rhetorical_move: statistical inventory from the Office of the Bar Confidant followed by three illustrative case summaries

The 'Lahar Division': when he joined the Court in 1995, all five members of his Third Division -- Feliciano, Romero, Melo, Vitug and himself -- were Kapampangans, and he is now its only surviving member.

The statues at the Supreme Court's gate: Jose Abad Santos, who chose martyrdom over collaboration with the Japanese, and Cayetano Arellano, the first Chief Justice, the only two magistrates so honored.

His own practice of footnoting in every ponencia the names of the attorneys who signed the parties' memoranda, sometimes with a brief comment on their work, and his request for a list of IBP-Pampanga members so he can speak well of them.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 12 of 'Judicial Renaissance' reproduces the address Justice Panganiban gave at the induction of the IBP-Pampanga Chapter's officers, opening with thanks to Judge Irin Zenaida S. Buan, who introduced him by analyzing his legal philosophy from his decisions rather than reciting his biography. He praised the new breed of Pampango magistrates, recalled the province's place in a century of judicial history through Chief Justices Jose Abad Santos and Cayetano Arellano, and remembered that when he joined the Court in 1995 all five members of his Third Division were cabalens -- the 'Lahar Division,' of which he is now the only survivor. Amid what he called a national crisis of confidence and credibility, he sounded a call to ethics built on three virtues. Fairness, he said, means refusing to take undue advantage of the other side, which he illustrated with the 1960 hearing where, standing in for an indisposed Dean Jovito R. Salonga, he was spared cross-examination because opposing counsel Jose W. Diokno moved to postpone the case in fairness to a young compañero. Candor means admitting error and conceding when a passage is a mere obiter, and never misquoting a decision, since eagle-eyed magistrates detect misquotation. Integrity means acting on what is true and honest regardless of consequences; he asked lawyers to denounce corrupt and incompetent judges, to defend decent ones from scurrilous attacks and baseless administrative complaints that stall promotions, and to condemn lawyers who collect money from clients ostensibly to pay off magistrates, insisting that corruption survives only where the bar abets or tolerates it. He then reported the Office of the Bar Confidant's figures for 1999 to 2004 -- 463 lawyers disciplined, 23 of them disbarred -- and summarized three recent cases of estate fraud, obstinate immorality and deliberate deception of a trial court. Quoting Justice J. B. L. Reyes on keeping one's soul attuned to morality and honor, he developed the figure of a mariner's compass permanently calibrated to the north, warned against technicians who invert the hierarchy of loyalties, and closed by urging cabalen attorneys to keep no compass but ethics, no master but law, no guide but honor and no aim but justice.
